question_text:
Restoration ecologist Teodora Valcourt monitors six replanted wetland sites, tallying the cumulative number of plant species recorded at each site since replanting. Valcourt argues that Pelham Flat differs from the other five sites in the pace of its gains: its average number of species added per year was lower during the later stretch of monitoring (years 5 to 11) than during the middle stretch (years 2 to 5), whereas at every other site the later pace was equal to or higher than the middle pace.

Which choice best describes data from the table that support Valcourt's argument?
answer_a: Pelham Flat had the lowest species total of the six sites after 11 years of monitoring.
answer_b: Pelham Flat added fewer species between years 5 and 11 than any of the other five sites did.
answer_c: Pelham Flat's average yearly gain between years 5 and 11 was half its average yearly gain between years 2 and 5, a drop that no other site showed.
answer_d: Between years 2 and 5, Pelham Flat added more species than any of the other five sites did.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. The table gives cumulative totals over stretches of unequal length (3 years from year 2 to year 5, and 6 years from year 5 to year 11), so each gain must be divided by the length of its stretch. Pelham Flat added 12 species in each stretch, which is 4 per year in the middle stretch but only 2 per year in the later one, half the pace. At the other sites the later pace was never lower: Dunmore Fen 6 then 6 per year, Tarn Basin 5 then 5, Wren Hollow 4 then 6, Cobb Landing 3 then 5, Ashby Cut 4 then 7. Only Pelham Flat slowed.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It is true (Pelham Flat's 44 species is below Cobb Landing's 45 and every other site's total), but a final total says nothing about when the species were added, so it does not show that Pelham Flat's gains came early rather than late.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It is true (Pelham Flat added 12 species from year 5 to year 11, fewer than any other site), but it compares raw gains across sites and says nothing about how Pelham Flat's yearly pace in this stretch compares with its own pace earlier, which is what the argument is about.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It is false: Pelham Flat added 12 species between years 2 and 5, but Dunmore Fen added 18 and Tarn Basin added 15.

question_text:
After an unusually wet harvest season, agricultural scientist Ingrid Faulkner-Osei inspected grain lots held in six types of on-farm storage across a farming region. For each storage type, she recorded how many lots she inspected and the percentage of those lots that showed visible mold. Reviewing her records, Faulkner-Osei concluded that flat warehouses had the greatest total number of lots with visible mold in her sample.

Which choice best describes data from the table that support Faulkner-Osei's conclusion?
answer_a: Although wooden cribs had the highest percentage of lots with visible mold and concrete silos had the most lots inspected, flat warehouses had more lots with visible mold than any other storage type.
answer_b: Wooden cribs had a higher percentage of lots with visible mold than any other storage type did.
answer_c: Concrete silos had far more lots inspected than any other storage type, so the silos must have produced the most moldy lots.
answer_d: Plastic liner bags and earthen pits each had at least 40 percent of their lots show visible mold, a higher percentage than flat warehouses had.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. The conclusion concerns the number of moldy lots, not the rate of mold, so each percentage must be applied to its group's size. Multiplying gives about 99 moldy lots for concrete silos (11 percent of 900), 133 for steel bins (38 percent of 350), 33 for wooden cribs (55 percent of 60), 140 for flat warehouses (28 percent of 500), 64 for plastic liner bags (40 percent of 160), and 36 for earthen pits (45 percent of 80). Flat warehouses therefore produced the most moldy lots, even though wooden cribs had the highest mold percentage and concrete silos had the most lots inspected.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The statement is accurate (55 percent for wooden cribs is the highest rate), but a high percentage says nothing about how many lots were moldy. Wooden cribs had only 60 lots inspected, so about 33 moldy lots, the fewest of any type. This reads the percentage column alone and ignores group size.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. Concrete silos did have the most lots inspected (900), but only 11 percent of those lots showed mold, the lowest rate in the table, which gives about 99 moldy lots. That is fewer than the roughly 140 moldy lots for flat warehouses and about 133 for steel bins. A large number of lots inspected does not by itself mean a large number of moldy lots.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. The statement is accurate (40 percent and 45 percent are both higher than 28 percent), but it compares only rates. Plastic liner bags and earthen pits had just 160 and 80 lots inspected, about 64 and 36 moldy lots, so a higher rate there does not mean more moldy lots than the roughly 140 from flat warehouses.

question_text:
Fisheries biologist Odalys Whitfern studies five salmon hatcheries on the Kessock River system. For each hatchery she recorded the number of eggs collected from spawning adults in one season and the number of fry the hatchery released into the river that same season. Whitfern hypothesizes that Cutbank, although it released fewer fry than Marrow, made better use of the eggs it collected than Marrow did.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Whitfern's hypothesis?
answer_a: Marrow collected more eggs than any other hatchery and released more fry than every hatchery except Pike Run.
answer_b: Marrow's fry total exceeded Cutbank's by a smaller factor than Marrow's egg total exceeded Cutbank's.
answer_c: Marrow's fry total exceeded Cutbank's by a larger factor than Marrow's egg total exceeded Cutbank's.
answer_d: Marrow's fry total exceeded Hollis's by a smaller factor than Marrow's egg total exceeded Hollis's.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it correctly compares Marrow and Cutbank, the two hatcheries named in the hypothesis, on both measures. Marrow released 90 thousand fry compared with Cutbank's 50 thousand, 1.8 times as many, but Marrow collected 150 thousand eggs compared with Cutbank's 80 thousand, 1.875 times as many. Because Marrow's fry total grew by a smaller factor than its egg total, a smaller portion of Marrow's eggs became released fry (60 percent) than of Cutbank's (62.5 percent), which supports the claim that Cutbank made better use of its eggs even though it released fewer fry.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The statement is accurate (Marrow collected the most eggs, 150 thousand, and its 90 thousand fry trail only Pike Run's 100 thousand), but it compares Marrow with all the hatcheries by raw totals and says nothing about how Cutbank's fry total relates to its egg total, so it does not bear on whether Cutbank used its eggs better.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. This reverses the comparison. Marrow's fry total exceeded Cutbank's by a factor of 1.8, which is smaller, not larger, than the factor of 1.875 by which Marrow's egg total exceeded Cutbank's.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It applies the right comparison to the wrong hatchery. Marrow's fry total (90 thousand) exceeded Hollis's (40 thousand) by a factor of 2.25, which is larger than the factor of 1.5 by which Marrow's egg total (150 thousand) exceeded Hollis's (100 thousand), and Hollis is not one of the hatcheries named in the hypothesis.

visual_data.title: Eggs collected and fry released by hatchery, one season
